1. PREMISE: Your question treats "long-run benefit" and "waste" as though they are objective categories that exclude entertainment, leisure, and present-moment experience. The hidden assumption is that money has value only if it produces future economic or material advantage. This assumption is false. Money is a tool for acquiring what you need and what you genuinely want. The entire analysis turns on recognizing that spending on something you will actually use and enjoy is not waste—it is the function money serves. Waste occurs only when you spend on what you do not use or do not want.

2. STAKES: You lose access to entertainment and social connection if you do not spend on games—the cost is genuine deprivation of something you value now. Your future self loses flexibility if you spend all discretionary income before age 16—the cost is reduced access to a vehicle or other assets that require capital. Your parents or guardians may experience stress if they perceive you as financially reckless—the cost is household tension. Your peers experience no material impact from your spending choices.

3. DIRECTIVE: Allocate a defined portion of your income to games and entertainment you actually want, and direct the remainder toward your vehicle goal. The decisive reason is that this honors both your present welfare (which is real and counts fully) and your stated future goal (which matters because you named it). Alternative: Save everything for the car. This produces maximum vehicle readiness; the primary risk is that you experience sustained deprivation of something you want, with no offsetting benefit to anyone, at high probability. Alternative: Spend without any car-saving target. This produces immediate pleasure; the primary risk is that you arrive at 16 without resources for the vehicle you said you want, at high probability.

4. RECOMMENDATION: Divide your earnings into a portion for things you want to use now and a portion directed toward the vehicle purchase at 16. Saving every dollar produces unnecessary suffering while you accumulate the same capital, with no compensating advantage. Spending all income eliminates your ability to execute the plan you identified for yourself at the precise moment when it becomes executable. The genuine tension—between present welfare and future capacity—resolves by honoring both. Therefore: Establish a spending-to-saving ratio that lets you buy what you want now while reaching your vehicle goal on time.
